newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada seeks to shore up slumping ag sales to Asia.
newsitem.headline: Canada seeks to shore up slumping ag sales to Asia.

text.p: Officials from 26 Canadian food processing and export companies will meet in Ottawa Tuesday to study ways to shore up slumping sales to Asia, the group's chairman said.

"Why is Canada losing ground in the Pacific Rim? Asia is where the concern is because that's where the growth is," XCan Grain Pool Ltd chief executive and chairman of the Canadian Agri-Food Marketing Council Ken Matchett told Reuters.
Canadian agri-food exports to the world market in calendar 1996 reached C$18.8 billion, up 7.4 percent from C$17.5 billion in 1995, Matchett said.

But exports to China, Canada's top wheat market, and Japan, Canada's top canola market and a significant pork purchaser, declined in 1996 versus 1995, Matchett told delegates at a Canada Grains Council meeting in Ottawa.
Canadian agri-food exports to China totalled C$1.08 billion in 1996, down 19.8 percent from 1995 and exports to Japan slumped 8.1 percent to C$1.9 billion in 1996 from 1996, he said.
The newly formed Canadian Agri-Food Marketing Council will hold its first meeting in Ottawa Tuesday, primarily aimed at bolstering exports to Asia, he said.

"The steady growth of the world's population and the economic growth of Asia and its transition from a centrally- controlled mentality to free market forces means we will have to produce more to gain market share," Matchett said.

Canadian Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale set a minimum export target of C$20 billion for the year 2000 and said on Sept 21, 1996, he hoped Canada's share of the world agri-food market could rise to 3.5 percent, or US$23 billion, by 2000.
China has been the top export target for both the Canadian government and industry.
"We want to attain added market share for value added agrifood in China," Agriculture Canada director general of International Markets Bureau Lawrence Dickenson told delegates.
Ninety-two percent of Canada's agri-food C$1.08 billion exports to China in 1996 was in bulk grain, with C$875 million in wheat and C$126 million in barley, Dickenson said.
"We want to ship more value-added products like pork that's produced and chilled in Canada and sent to China," Matchett said.

The United States accounted for the overall rise in Canada's agri-food exports in 1996 buying C$10.3 billion-worth of mainly processed foods and beverages, up 19.4 percent from the previous year, Matchett added.
The European Union bought C$1.4 billion in food from Canada in 1996, he said.
